title: Coronavirus Economic Response Package (Jobkeeper Payments) Amendment Bill 2020
short_title: Coronavirus Economic Response Package (Jobkeeper Payments) Amendment Bill 2020

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would extend the JobKeeper payment scheme until 28 March 2021.
It would allow protected JobKeeper information to be shared with Australian government agencies for coronavirus-related law administration.
The bill would also extend the period for making a related information sharing determination under the Omnibus Act.
changes: Extends the JobKeeper payment period to 28 March 2021.
Amends tax secrecy provisions to permit disclosure of JobKeeper information to government agencies for coronavirus purposes.
Extends the period for a related information sharing determination.
summary.affected: Australian government agencies and participants in the JobKeeper scheme.

divisions.question: Andrew Leigh We are now in the greatest economic downturn that Australia has seen since the Great Depression. Research from the Australian Treasury has revealed just how damaging this can be, particularly to young Australians. That research has looked at the so-called scarring effect, the long-term effect, of graduating in the teeth of a recession. I know this effect well, having finished high school in 1990 and seen some of my classmates who searched for work utterly unable to find it at that time. We know now that there are 13 jobseekers for every job vacancy, so this problem is particularly acute. The research conducted by Daniel Andrews of the Australian Treasury—now at the OECD—titled _The career effect of labour market conditions of entry_ found that a person who enters the labour market for the first time during a recession is more likely to be unemployed and more likely to be unemployed for longer. When they do find a job—if they do—they are more likely to work at a low-productivity firm and are less likely to switch firms, thereby missing out on the wage gains that come from that. Their estimate is that somebody who enters the workforce in a year in which youth unemployment is five percentage points higher suffers an eight per cent hit to their earnings in the first year and a 3.5 per cent hit to their earnings in the fifth year. The scarring effect lasts a full decade. We know that in Australia right now we are seeing significant adverse effects right across the labour market. We've seen a downturn in hours of some 20 per cent and the effective unemployment rate, the Treasurer tells us, will go to 13 per cent. The difference between those is JobKeeper, a wage subsidy scheme urged on the government, after they initially dragged their heels, by Labor. Labor recognises the value of wage subsidy schemes and maintaining the connection between employer and employee. Its value has been shown in Australia, as it has overseas. Mehreen Faruqi I rise to continue my speech on the Coronavirus Economic Response Package (Jobkeeper Payments) Amendment Bill 2020. Women are already bearing the brunt of the economic impacts of the pandemic—so much so that economists have said that we are in a pink collar recession. Women lost their jobs twice as fast as men when the economy was shut down. Women are over-represented as casual workers and in industries most affected by shutdowns like retail and hospitality. Women are under-represented in the few industries which received targeted stimulus, such as the construction sector. Young women have been forced to dip into their already meagre superannuation balances at disproportionate rates to make it through the crisis, which is going to decimate their retirement savings. The government's approach to early childhood education and care was a double whammy for women and their earning potential. Not only did the government rip away access to free child care—potentially one of the most significant boosts to women's capacity to enter and remain in the workforce in a generation—but it carved the highly feminised early learning and care workforce out of JobKeeper altogether, months before the scheme was originally scheduled to end. There has been no job creation for women during this crisis and there is none planned for the recovery. Instead, women have been totally shafted and left to fend for themselves. I've said it before and I'll say it again: our recovery plans must have women at the front and centre of planning and decision-making. This recovery must be a feminist recovery. Creating this two-tier JobKeeper system will also be a disaster. Can I remind the chamber that we are in the middle of a pandemic and in the middle of a recession. This is not the time to be cutting the critical JobKeeper payment, which is $1,500 at the moment; it's really barely a living wage to begin with. The government is shifting the cost of supporting businesses onto ordinary workers. Why should the pay of workers go down when the business's revenue is improving? speeches.speaker: Jim Chalmers
speeches.brief: The speaker supported extending JobKeeper but criticised the Treasurer's sole control over rates and eligibility, noting that millions of workers—including casuals, aviation and university staff—remain excluded, and argued the government is withdrawing support too quickly without a jobs plan, moving an amendment to tailor rates to rising unemployment.

speeches.speaker: Madeleine King
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the amendment and bill but argued the Morrison government’s response to COVID-19 was painfully slow, poorly implemented, and excluded millions, citing 520,000 payroll jobs lost, 400,000 additional workers expected to lose jobs by Christmas, a $60 billion JobKeeper bungle, and $33 billion in superannuation withdrawals. The speaker criticised the government for failing to include aviation workers, universities, and international students in JobKeeper, and for lacking a comprehensive jobs plan.

speeches.speaker: Matt Keogh
speeches.brief: The government's planned reductions to JobKeeper and JobSeeker are premature without a comprehensive jobs plan, and support should be extended and expanded to excluded industries like childcare, hospitality, arts, and local government. The speech notes 520,000 payroll jobs lost, a predicted further 400,000, and that JobKeeper rates will drop from $1,500 to as low as $650 per fortnight by early 2021, while the government has room in its revised $101 billion cost estimate to do more.

speeches.speaker: Anika Wells
speeches.brief: The speech welcomed the JobKeeper extension to March 2021 but criticised the scheme's implementation for excluding childcare, university, casual and dnata workers. It cited 2.7 million people withdrawing $33.3 billion from superannuation, Qantas's outsourcing of 2,500 ground crew jobs, and projected 400,000 further job losses by Christmas, arguing for a comprehensive jobs plan.

speeches.speaker: Brendan O'Connor
speeches.brief: The speaker supported extending JobKeeper but argued the government's eligibility criteria were too narrow and the support came too late, and criticised a provision allowing recovered businesses to unilaterally cut employee hours by up to 40%.

speeches.speaker: Bert van Manen
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Coronavirus Economic Response Package (Jobkeeper Payments) Amendment Bill 2020, arguing for the extension of JobKeeper payments until 28 March 2021 with a two-tiered payment system and revised turnover tests, citing that over 5,300 organisations in the electorate of Forde benefited and provided examples like Club Beenleigh retaining 32 staff, Good Life Kindergarten retaining nine, and Harvey's Towing retaining 29.

speeches.speaker: Catherine King
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the JobKeeper extension amendments but argued that the bill still leaves behind aviation, arts, council, casual, and childcare workers, specifically citing Qantas outsourcing 2,500 jobs and dnata workers being denied support. They criticised the government for lacking a long-term aviation plan and for allowing unilateral 40% hour reductions for workers in recovered businesses.

speeches.speaker: Tony Pasin
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Coronavirus Economic Response Package (Jobkeeper Payments) Amendment Bill 2020, arguing that JobKeeper was the most significant measure for saving livelihoods and noting that 3,700 businesses in his electorate had used it, including specific employers like Josslyn Lee and Lucy Von Stanke’s cafe, Karen Milesi’s hotel, Tom Kosch’s motel, Toni Vorenas’s bakery, and Thyme at the Lakes.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Labor proposed amendments to the JobKeeper extension bill to ensure workers whose hours are cut do not receive less than the $750-a-week JobKeeper rate and to deny emergency industrial relations powers to businesses not receiving the subsidy. Labor also highlighted the initial rejection of wage subsidies and the $60 billion JobKeeper overpayment mistake under Treasurer Josh Frydenberg.

speeches.speaker: Patrick Conaghan
speeches.brief: The speaker supported extending the JobKeeper payment for another six months and retesting eligibility to target businesses most in need, citing the $70 billion package as having helped retain staff and citing positive feedback from businesses such as Dorrigo Hotel, Settlers Inn, Observatory Apartments, and McGrath real estate.

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: The government was forced into supporting JobKeeper after initially resisting, but one million casual workers were excluded; the speaker argued that cutting JobKeeper is premature and called for a green-led recovery with investment in renewable energy and domestic manufacturing to combat the worst recession since the Great Depression.

speeches.speaker: Helen Haines
speeches.brief: The member for Indi supported the extension of JobKeeper until 28 March 2021, citing that over 4,600 businesses in her electorate received the payment in May, and argued for amendments to include universities and childcare sectors, while presenting a budget submission for regional tourism and infrastructure projects.

speeches.speaker: Peta Murphy
speeches.brief: The speech argued for extending JobKeeper, criticised the government for initially refusing and delaying the scheme, and highlighted specific workers and businesses in Dunkley left out or facing hardship, while opposing the extension of emergency industrial relations powers that could weaken worker protections.

speeches.speaker: Zali Steggall
speeches.brief: The member for Warringah welcomed the JobKeeper extension to March 2021 but urged targeted support for travel agents, events, arts, entertainment, and childcare industries, and called for eligibility clarifications for start-ups and sole traders, along with greater attention to women and youth disproportionately affected by the economic downturn.

speeches.speaker: Ben Morton
speeches.brief: The bill extends the JobKeeper payment until 28 March 2021, introduces a two-tiered payment rate to better align with part-time hours, and extends temporary Fair Work Act provisions for employer flexibility. Legacy employers must meet a 10% decline in turnover test to access modified provisions, with penalties for providing false information.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Labor argued that the government was reluctant to introduce wage subsidies, leading to hundreds of thousands of unnecessary job losses, and criticised the rejection of amendments that would prevent workers from being paid less than JobKeeper recipients, citing a gap between $314 billion and $85 billion in claimed economic support.
